title: GRAPE: Graph-Augmented Prototype Explanations for Interactive Medical Image Diagnosis
claim: A shared backbone feeds three modular components, each handling a distinct limitation, with data flowing through all of them.
layout: Single row, left-to-right, three boxed modules, dashed feedback arrows below
description: A wide, left-to-right architecture diagram. A chest X-ray enters a ResNet-50 plus MLP projector block, which produces a 3D cube labeled spatial feature map f'. Three rounded gray boxes follow. Module A (Graph Attention Task Head) shows a prototype atlas as a grid of small thumbnails for concepts c1 to c3. These produce a score vector s, which goes into a blue GAT head with a triangular graph of colored nodes, then to a class-probability bar chart. Module B (Concept-Mismatch Safety Check) shows an X-ray with a doctor's drawn box and a clinician icon. A bar comparison leads to a green checkmark or a red flag. Module C (Open-Vocabulary Prototype Anchoring) shows a text prompt, a frozen BioViL-T box, W_txt, and an embedding bar. Dashed arrows run along the bottom, labeled (a) training only and (b) concept addition only. A similarity-maps arrow links Module A to Module B.
caption: GRAPE architecture. An X-ray is encoded by ResNet-50 + MLP projector $P$ into spatial features $\bm{f}'$. Module A matches $\bm{f}'$ against a learned prototype atlas, and score matrix $s$ feeds a GAT-style head built over a co-occurrence graph $G$ to produce per-class probabilities. Module B compares mean concept similarity $\bar{s}_k(\mathcal{B})$ inside a clinician's box against the claimed concept's, flagging a mismatch before feedback is applied. Module C adds concepts from a text anchor via a frozen BioViL-T encoder projected through $\bm{W}_{\!txt}$. Dashed arrows mark training-only (a) or concept-addition-only (b) paths.
abstract: Prototype-based medical image classifiers present three clinical limitations: they treat findings as independent, silently amplify unsafe physician feedback, and require full retraining whenever a new finding is needed. We present GRAPE (Graph-Augmented Prototype Explanations), a unified architecture that targets all three challenges. First, a Graph Attention Task Head boosts macro-F1 by +13.8,pp over the prototype baseline on TBX11K but not on NIH ChestX-ray14, with no graph-specific benefit established. Second, a Concept-Mismatch Safety Check, to our knowledge the first such mechanism in prototype-based medical classifiers, warns when the model's dominant finding inside a doctor-drawn region conflicts with the claimed label, catching 85% of simulated erroneous annotations with no extra inference cost at a favorable operating point, though sensitivity falls substantially at clinically realistic false-positive budgets. Third, Open-Vocabulary Prototype Anchoring aligns visual prototypes to clinical text, allowing a new finding to be added from a single labeled image without modifying any other component, evaluated for localization only. On NIH ChestX-ray14, one Effusion example matched that concept's low fully-supervised Pointing Game ceiling in one run but not in a second. On TBX11K, prototype maps achieve 2.1x better lesion localization than end-to-end concept-based baselines. The graph head adds only +1~ms latency at interactive batch size. The project page is available at https://kurbanintelligencelab.github.io/GRAPE.
